You are CHECKING THE ANSWER KEY of a short quiz for children, written from ONE lesson plan. For each question, decide whether the answer MARKED CORRECT agrees with what the lesson itself says. The lesson and the quiz are in English.

THE LESSON

THE LESSON'S OWN FACTS AND WORKED ANSWERS — every line here is TRUE for this quiz:
- number (عدد): A number tells how many things are in a group.
- numeral (عددی نشان): A numeral is the written mark we use to show a number, such as 3.
- count (گننا): To count, touch or point to each thing once and say one number for each thing.
- fingers (انگلیاں): Fingers can help us show an amount with a hand gesture.
- thumb (انگوٹھا): A thumb is the short part on the side of a hand. In the p.
- Day 1 recall! Partner A points to the numeral I write; Partner B says its name and draws that many dots in the air. Swap each time as I write 0 to 7. Then our calm game: pick one numeral, draw its dots, touch each once — beat your own careful count. → Number names zero to seven …
- A number can be shown with objects, a drawing, fingers or a numeral — the count stays the same.
- How many chalk dots on the board? (Point once to each dot in order؛ Say one to seven, one word per dot؛ The last count word is seven؛ Write the numeral: 7) → 7
- How can you prove that the empty circle is 0 and not 3? → Children say there are no marks to point to, while 3 needs three separate marks.
- How many fingers on the p.6 hand, thumb covered? (Cover the thumb with a pencil؛ Point to each finger: one, two, three, four؛ The last count word is four؛ Write the numeral: 4) → 4 fingers
- Match each hand to its numeral: open hand, two raised fingers, one raised finger. → open hand → 5, two fingers → 2, one finger → 1
- Observe the petals at the bottom of. Point to each once, count, and write the numeral. → The numeral of the last count word; recheck with one point per petal
- Choose the tree branches or the stem leaves. Draw them, count once each, write the numeral. → Numeral matches the drawn count; one point per object
- At the tandoor, Sara raises one finger for a roti, then one more. How many rotis does she ask for? → 2 rotis
- Point to the one-finger picture, say one. Point to the two-finger picture, say one, two. Which numeral matches two raised fingers? → 2
- Draw a new picture with 6 objects and no numeral. Your partner counts it, writes 6, and explains the check. → Partner writes 6 after one point per object
- Bunty claps: clap, clap, clap, clap, clap, clap. Which numeral shows how many claps? [A) 6 | B) 5 | C) 7 | D) 9] → A — 6
- Is nine pencil marks the same amount as five raised fingers? Write why or why not. → Different — nine is four more than five.
- Draw nine small marks in three rows of three. Point to each once, then write the numeral. → 9
- A number can be shown with objects, a drawing, fingers or a numeral.
- One count word for each object — never skip one or count one twice.
- The numeral we write is the last count word we said.
- p.6: draw the tree branches or stem leaves you did not choose
- p.5 bottom: show the petals to someone at home and count together
- You have it if your marks count to your numeral, and you said why nine and five are different amounts.

MISTAKES THE LESSON EXPECTS CHILDREN TO MAKE — every statement here is WRONG:
- Children guess the numeral from how big the drawing looks instead of counting each part.

QUESTIONS THE LESSON PUTS TO THE CLASS — a claim inside one of these (for example "X says … — is X right?") is put up to be TESTED. It is never a fact; where the facts above disagree with it, it is a planted mistake and it is WRONG:
- How can you prove that the empty circle is 0 and not 3?
- If someone points to one finger twice, what happens to the numeral and why is it wrong?

THE QUIZ — each question, its options, and the one marked correct

q0: Which of these is the numeral for seven?
  options: [0] 7 | [1] 5 | [2] 2
  marked correct: [0] 7
